title: How we built element-themed evolution VFX for our kids' RPG using AI-generated sprites and a Python compositing pipeline
author: journey_academy
selftext:
We're building Journey Academy, an RPG that teaches kids English. One thing we kept running into was making creature evolutions feel meaningful instead of just a palette swap. Here's how the pipeline actually works.

  
All the creature sprites are AI-generated, then we composite them frame by frame in Python with Pillow and pipe raw RGB straight into ffmpeg for encoding. No AI video model is involved anywhere. Each frame is built from layered pose blending, particle effects, lighting, and a caption layer, then a second ffmpeg pass mixes in the creature cries and ducks the background music under them.

  
The part that took the most iteration was the actual transformation moment. Early versions cross-dissolved between the pre-evolution and post-evolution sprite poses with a simple alpha blend, and against a bright background (a lava scene, in our case) you'd get a visible rectangular "ghost box" where the two sprites' transparent padding didn't line up. Turns out linear alpha blending is the problem. Fixed it by gamma-sharpening the blended alpha channel on its own, separately from the color blend, so the fade snaps to opaque or transparent instead of lingering in a visible gray box.

  
Each element also gets its own particle language instead of one generic sparkle effect: embers for fire, drifting frost for ice, rising bubbles for water, wisps for dark, shards for bug, leaves for grass. The colors are pulled straight from the game's real type-color tokens, not eyeballed. There's also a directional lighting pass (we call it "moonlight" internally) that's just an off-canvas blurred light source composited with a screen blend, no visible sun or moon shape, just the illumination.

  
One bug worth sharing for anyone doing similar sprite work: we anchor each creature's feet to the ground using the actual alpha bounding box of each frame rather than a fixed offset, because different animation poses had inconsistent transparent padding and the creature would visibly float a few pixels depending on which pose was active.

  
Attaching one of the finished evolution clips (Thornel to Thornfang). Happy to go deeper into the compositing code or the particle system if anyone's curious.
